raw_response:
I will start from what worked for me before, then make small changes. My land is only 3.8 mu, so every bag of fertilizer costs real money, but I still will not cut too hard on fertilizer because if chili drops yield, that hurts more than spending a bit extra. I have well water, so I can push chili a little more than dryland people. Chili is my cash crop, so I will put most of the land into chili and keep a smaller piece in maize for steadier grain and to spread risk. For chili, I will use hybrid seed, make the base fertilizer heavier, then topdress in splits after it starts growing strong and again after first picking. I will keep phosphorus and potassium up because chili needs fruit setting and color, not just leaves. I will water more often for chili, especially after transplanting, flowering, and fruit expansion. I know from nearby growers that if water and fertilizer are short, chili stays small and picking is not worth the labor. For maize, I will keep it simpler: one good base application, one topdress around jointing, fewer sprays, and fewer irrigations. I usually look at what other people around me do, and I do not want to fall below the common level. Since some family members work off-farm, I also need a plan that my household can actually manage, so I will use rotary tillage for both crops because it is quicker and cheaper than deep ploughing every time.
